title: CamelBak: water on your back—why bite the outlet? | Brand Stories
description:
Once water is on your back, how do you get it out when you want a drink and keep it in place otherwise? Follow the brand's sock-and-clothespin account through a mouthpiece patent, a bottle at a 2006 trade show, a 2015 lab report, a 2016 engineer's recollection, and current sealing and drying guidance. The race organizer's retrospective gives conflicting 1988/1989 dates; neither is selected. The company's 1989 founding is a separate event. Patent designs, observed products and samples from different periods are not treated as one SKU, batch or historical first. Test procedures are not durability results. Visuals are original anonymous concept illustrations; media has not yet been generated.

thumbnail.headline:
The outlet
must close itself
thumbnail.sub: How to reuse a bag of water

chapters.c14r1h01: Water on your back—who controls the outlet?
chapters.c14r1o01: From a clothespin to a self-closing slit
chapters.c14r1b01: The outlet moves to a handheld bottle
chapters.c14r1t01: Twisting bags and repeatedly squeezing valves
chapters.c14r1m01: A mold produces a silicone part you can test
chapters.c14r1r01: The mouthpiece is shut, but the cap can still leak
chapters.c14r1d01: The last water must leave the corners

c14r1h01.text: You carry three liters of water, but if the tube keeps dripping, it leaks away before you drink. Can carrying more water solve that?

c14r1h02.text: In the late 1980s, at a Texas bike race, Eidson put a bag of water behind his cycling jersey, according to the brand's retrospective.

c14r1h03.text: A sock covered the bag, and a tube ran over his shoulder. What caught my eye was the clothespin at the tube's end.

c14r1h04.text: Later, the outlet was clamped between metal pieces that simulated teeth.

c14r1h07.text: In another case study, an engineer made a mold for the mouthpiece.

c14r1h05.text: Today, follow a bag of CamelBak water from carrying it on your back to being able to drink from it again next time.

c14r1h06.text: Once water is on your back, how do you let it out when you want a drink and keep it where it belongs the rest of the time?

c14r1o01.text: In the brand's New Zealand retrospective I read, Eidson used that clothespin to clamp the tube's outlet.

c14r1o02.text: He was an emergency medical technician. The water bag in that account had originally been an IV bag.

c14r1o04.text: But is moving the outlet to your mouth the same as making it close itself?

c14r1o05.text: This improvised setup still needed manual clamping. Someone had to handle the clothespin; it would not return to the tube simply because you finished drinking.

c14r1o07.text: If the outlet closed when you released it from your mouth, would your hands have one less thing to manage?

c14r1v01.text: Later bite valves gave the mouth control of that switch. One mouthpiece patent records a deformable outlet.

c14r1v02.text: The application was filed in 1998 and granted in 2000. Its outlet is not a round hole that stays open all the time.

c14r1v03.text: Two touching sections at the front form a normally closed slit. The water path is connected, but the slit has not opened.

c14r1v04.text: If you only think about making the hole bigger, you miss a question: who closes that hole when you are not drinking?

c14r1v05.text: In the patent, teeth press the bite region, deforming the mouthpiece. The two touching sections separate to form an outlet.

c14r1v06.text: When that force is removed, elasticity returns it to a closed state. Opening and closing rely on the same part changing shape.

c14r1v07.text: I like that change: the external clothespin gives way to a shape within the outlet that returns by itself.

c14r1v08.text: But if the material is soft enough to bite, why doesn't it stay flattened after you let go?

c14r1v09.text: The document selects material for its ability to return to a closed state and gives silicone of a particular hardness as an example. It must be soft yet spring back.

c14r1v10.text: The mouthpiece's neck connects to the tube, and its head goes in your mouth. How do you clean the bit that touches your mouth all day?

c14r1v11.text: The patent says the mouthpiece can slide off the tube and be put back on, making cleaning and maintenance easier.

c14r1v13.text: The document also records a flow test. Once you bite open this slit, how can water pass through?

c14r1v14.text: It uses the mouthpiece shown in Figures 1 through 10: put it in your mouth, bite it into the flow position, then suck as if through a straw.

c14r1v15.text: The patent applicant reports a flow of about 35 to 45 milliliters per second. That figure includes the user's sucking action.

c14r1v16.text: What interests me most here is that the water path finally has an observable result: the mouth opens the outlet while drawing water through it.

c14r1v17.text: This is the test recorded for that design. It does not mean every bag and every mouthpiece will deliver the same flow.

c14r1v18.text: But with control now at your mouth, does the water still have to stay on your back?

c14r1b01.text: In a 2006 trade-show report, that bite-to-drink outlet had moved onto a clear water bottle.

c14r1b02.text: The reporter describes a 750-milliliter bottle with a flip-up bite valve and a short straw connected beneath it inside the bottle.

c14r1b03.text: You have a bottle in your hand again, without returning to an open bottle mouth. That is what made me pause.

c14r1b05.text: The container has changed. Can the job of opening only when you drink move with it?

c14r1b06.text: A bottle application published that same year describes a bite mouthpiece that deforms under pressure and cites the earlier mouthpiece patent.

c14r1b07.text: Its idea is still to press open and release to close. Changing the container need not mean starting over with the switching principle.

c14r1b08.text: But when the report calls it leakproof, did the reporter test that, or was it the company's claim?

c14r1b09.text: Leakproof was the company's description in the report. This exhibit brought the division of work between outlet and container to an everyday bottle.

c14r1b11.text: Still, is drinking once from a bottle the same test as repeatedly squeezing a bag on your body and biting its valve?

c14r1t01.text: A carried bag gets squeezed, and the water path has separate parts. The 2014 annual report describes that period's combination.

c14r1t02.text: It was a polyurethane reservoir, a tube and a self-sealing mouthpiece. The same report also lists polyurethane film in its procurement section.

c14r1t03.text: As you carry it, the bag bends, while a different small part at your mouth is repeatedly compressed.

c14r1t04.text: So, to examine repeated use, where should the force be applied?

c14r1t05.text: In 2015, a reporter visited the lab in Petaluma, California, and saw reservoirs being compressed and twisted.

c14r1t06.text: The metal teeth from the opening were two metal pieces clamping 12 bite valves, repeatedly simulating bites by adults and children.

c14r1t08.text: I think that scene deserves a closer look than a simple claim of durability.

c14r1t11.text: But the mouthpiece shape on a screen is not yet a soft part you can touch. How does an engineer first make it?

c14r1m01.text: A 2016 supplier case study interviewed design engineer McCready. He was making a one-piece, self-sealing silicone bite-valve sample.

c14r1m02.text: The mold from our opening was one he made by 3D printing, then used to produce silicone bite-valve samples.

c14r1m05.text: The engineer recalled getting test parts this way in just two days.

c14r1m07.text: I am more interested in what the engineer wanted to obtain after getting those soft samples.

c14r1m08.text: He said the more feedback they could get from testing with real people, the better.

c14r1m09.text: But even if the valve at your mouth seals itself, another opening must open for refilling. Can that one keep water in too?

c14r1r01.text: The refill opening brings you back to the bag. The current description of the reservoir from our opening specifically lists a handle for easy gripping and refilling.

c14r1r02.text: This model also has an on/off lever that lets you shut the drinking tube with one hand.

c14r1r03.text: I used to think keeping water in was all about that tiny piece at the mouth. But the refill cap is another joint that has to close properly.

c14r1r04.text: If the outlet is not dripping but water escapes around the cap, where would you look first?

c14r1r05.text: The maker's current FAQ lists two possible causes: grit in the cap threads, or a twisted sealing ring inside the cap.

c14r1r06.text: Grit prevents the cap from sealing fully. If that black ring twists out of shape, it can also compromise the seal.

c14r1r08.text: Can you expose that gap before carrying the bag outside?

c14r1r09.text: For its pre-season check, the maker says to fill the reservoir, close the cap, then rotate and squeeze it while watching for leaks.

c14r1r11.text: I think it stays with our original question: to take water with you, you also need to know whether it has already escaped somewhere else.

c14r1r12.text: But after drinking and washing, water should no longer remain inside. How do you get it out this time?

c14r1d01.text: Water left after washing tests the route in reverse. The maker's cleaning page says water may remain in corners, the drinking tube and the bite valve.

c14r1d02.text: Seeing a dry outside does not mean the inside of the tube and the seams have dried too.

c14r1d03.text: To me, this is the trickiest reversal in the whole route: keep water in while drinking, but get the remaining water out before storage.

c14r1d04.text: So the maker's cleaning guidance covers more than the large bag. The tube and mouthpiece that carried water need clean water too.

c14r1d05.text: But after the residue is washed away, if the inner walls still stick together, where can air get in?

c14r1d06.text: The cleaning page says to prop the reservoir open for ventilation. A drying rack separates the two inner walls and lets water drain.

c14r1d08.text: The maker says water may collect at low points if the tube is tightly coiled. How can you give the tube a route to dry too?

c14r1d09.text: It drains the tube, hangs it vertically and leaves both ends open. Drying is not just for the reservoir's interior.

c14r1d10.text: Drying the pieces separately uses removable parts. The space left for the tube and valve also lets you check whether water is still inside.

c14r1d11.text: One more look tells you whether it can be stored. What does the maker want you to check?

c14r1d12.text: Before storage, the maker asks you to check seams, corners, tubes and connections for droplets or condensation. If water remains, keep drying.

c14r1d13.text: We began by asking whether water can stay where it belongs. Here, the answer gains another moment: when you store it, the water must leave.

c14r1ct1.text: A bag of water becomes convenient when opening, closing and reuse form a connected route. The capacity sits on your back, but the outlets and joints still need care.

c14r1ct2.text: Do you most often take water cycling, walking, or keep it by your desk? Tell me in the comments which small detail matters most to you.

c14r1ct3.text: To see how familiar objects bring convenience to your hands, subscribe and join me in looking at the small actions that make them work.
